planting.note: In mild-winter regions sow in early fall for a winter-into-spring harvest; elsewhere direct sow around the last frost date.

directions: Broadcast or row sow seed clusters thickly and shallowly, since this type is grown for its abundant tender leaves rather than for large stalks. This unusual Italian chard lacks the thick, wide ribs of standard Swiss chard, instead producing slender stems and smooth, spinach-like leaves that regrow quickly after cutting. Favored by cooks for its mild flavor and quick-cooking texture, it tolerates both cool weather and mild heat better than many leafy greens, making it useful for extended cutting through a Gulf Coast winter.

common_name: Charlotte Swiss Chard (AAS-Winning Compact Red Chard)

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date, or start indoors and transplant a couple weeks after; also suitable for fall sowing in mild climates.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into rich soil and keep evenly watered, since this compact hybrid rewards close, container-friendly spacing. Named an All-America Selections winner, it produces bright cherry-red stalks and veins beneath glossy, deeply savoyed dark green leaves on a notably uniform, tidy plant. Its shorter stature and vigorous regrowth after cutting make it well suited to raised beds and pots as well as open garden rows.

common_name: Pink Lipstick Chard (Vivid Magenta-Stemmed Savoy Chard)

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date; in warm winter regions like the Gulf Coast also sow in fall for a winter harvest.

directions: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil and thin to final spacing, watering consistently to keep leaves tender through summer heat. Bred for its intensely saturated hot-pink stalks and veins, this selection stands out even among rainbow chard mixes and holds its color well after cooking. Its heavily crumpled, deep green leaves are produced over a long season, and repeated cutting encourages continued new growth from the crown.

planting.note: In zone 8-9 gardens sow in fall for a winter and early spring harvest; elsewhere sow 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost.

directions: Direct sow a half inch deep into cool, moist soil and thin seedlings once true leaves appear, harvesting outer leaves or whole plants as needed. This hybrid produces smooth to lightly crinkled, dark green leaves on a slow-to-bolt plant, making it a reliable choice for stretching the spring harvest window a bit longer than older heirloom types. It performs well as both a baby-leaf and full-size crop and holds quality in cool, short-day conditions common to winter gardening in the Gulf South.

planting.note: Sow in early fall while soil is still warm for a long fall-through-winter harvest window in mild-winter climates.

directions: Direct sow into well-drained beds and thin to stand a few inches apart, keeping soil consistently moist to support quick establishment in warm soil. This hybrid was bred with above-average heat tolerance and downy mildew resistance, allowing it to be sown earlier in fall or later into spring than many spinach types without bolting prematurely. Its dark green, savoyed leaves hold good texture and flavor even as temperatures rise, making it a strong pick for extending the cool-season window along the Gulf Coast.

planting.note: Sow in late summer to early fall for continued production into the warm shoulder season; can also be sown in early spring before heat sets in.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil and thin to final spacing, watering deeply to sustain the plant's large leaf size through warm weather. Named for its oversized, smooth blue-green leaves, this hybrid was selected specifically to resist bolting under longer days and warmer temperatures than most spinach can tolerate. It gives Gulf Coast growers a wider sowing window on either end of the cool season, holding productive quality later into spring and earlier into fall.

planting.note: Sow in fall for winter production in mild climates, or 4-5 weeks before the last spring frost elsewhere; good bolt tolerance allows a later spring sowing than most types.

directions: Direct sow shallowly into cool, moist soil and thin seedlings as they develop, harvesting the upright, easy-to-clean leaves individually or as whole plants. This hybrid forms a distinctly vertical rosette of smooth, dark green leaves that stay cleaner and easier to bunch than sprawling types, while its strong resistance to bolting extends the practical harvest window. Extension programs in warm-winter regions have recommended it for both fall and late-winter plantings where standard spinach would bolt too quickly.
